name: Madrid
meta_description: TDSC investigative consulting in matters touching Madrid: due diligence on Spanish groups, asset tracing and support around Madrid courts and arbitration.
hero_lede: Investigative consulting for matters that run through Madrid: Spanish and Latin American groups headquartered in the capital, disputes before Madrid's commercial courts and national courts, arbitrations administered in the city, and real estate and holding structures across the region. Scoped from Nashville with qualified Spanish professionals.
intro: Madrid is Spain's capital, its largest city and its main business centre. The city alone generated about 192.5 billion euros of GDP in 2024, around 12.1 percent of Spain's total, with services accounting for 89 percent of activity and advanced business services more than a quarter of gross value added. The Community of Madrid attracted 63.4 percent of foreign capital investment into Spain in the year to the fourth quarter of 2024. Large banks, energy, infrastructure, construction, telecommunications and insurance groups have their head offices here, alongside the national regulators, the Madrid stock exchange and the Adolfo Suarez Madrid-Barajas airport, Spain's main gateway to Latin America.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Madrid because it is where Spanish corporate decision-making, public contracting and much Ibero-American investment converge. Typical triggers include due diligence on Spanish groups and their Latin American subsidiaries, background research on executives and investment partners, support to counsel in shareholder, construction and financing disputes before Madrid courts or in arbitrations administered in the city, and asset tracing to enforce judgments and awards against parties holding real estate or companies in the region. Public procurement and concession risk around national ministries and infrastructure bodies, and inquiries into fraud or bribery that may reach the national criminal courts sitting in Madrid, are also recurring themes.

matters.title: Due diligence on Madrid-headquartered groups
matters.text: Ownership, management, litigation and regulatory history of Spanish groups and their subsidiaries in Spain and Latin America, using Mercantile Registry filings and the Official Gazette of the Mercantile Registry, published court decisions and regulator records, to support acquisitions, joint ventures and lending decisions.

matters.title: Arbitration support for Madrid cases
matters.text: Background research on counterparties, witnesses and experts and fact development for arbitrations administered in Madrid, including Ibero-American disputes, coordinated with counsel so that material can be assessed for use in the arbitration and in later annulment or enforcement proceedings.

matters.title: Asset tracing in the Madrid region
matters.text: Identification of real estate, companies and business interests connected to a judgment or award debtor in Madrid, combining corporate filings, Property Registry information obtained through counsel and open sources, to support enforcement planning by Spanish lawyers and court procedures.

matters.title: Public procurement and concession risk
matters.text: Screening of bidders, consortium partners, subcontractors and intermediaries on contracts awarded by national ministries, the regional government and infrastructure bodies based in Madrid, with attention to ownership opacity, prior sanctions or exclusions and links to politically exposed persons.

matters.title: Fraud and corruption inquiries
matters.text: Support to counsel investigating suspected fraud, bribery or market misconduct in Madrid entities, including matters that may reach the national criminal courts, scoped to respect Spanish employment and data protection rules and to preserve the evidential value of material gathered.

local_context.title: Commercial and civil courts
local_context.text: Madrid's specialised commercial courts deal with insolvency and company law matters arising in the region, with appeals to specialised sections of the Provincial Court of Madrid, while other civil and commercial claims go to the first-instance courts. Spain is reorganising first-instance courts into tribunales de instancia with specialised sections, so court names in recent filings may differ from older records and searches should cover both forms.

local_context.title: National courts in Madrid
local_context.text: As the capital, Madrid hosts the Supreme Court and the Audiencia Nacional, which has nationwide jurisdiction over certain serious offences, including major frauds affecting the national economy or more than one province. Large corporate fraud and corruption cases are therefore often investigated by central investigating courts in Madrid, making their published decisions and procedural records relevant to background and litigation research.

local_context.title: Madrid arbitration institutions
local_context.text: The Centro Internacional de Arbitraje de Madrid (CIAM) was created in 2020 from the international arbitration activity of the Corte de Arbitraje de Madrid, the Corte Civil y Mercantil de Arbitraje (CIMA) and the Corte Espanola de Arbitraje, with the Madrid Bar Association as strategic partner. Following integration with the Santiago de Chile chamber's arbitration court it presented the name CIIAM in early 2026, with seats in Madrid and Santiago. Domestic arbitrations continue before the founding institutions.

local_context.title: Registries and regional authorities
local_context.text: Companies seated in Madrid file with the Mercantile Registry of Madrid, part of the national registry system operated by the Registradores, and property is recorded in the local Property Registries. The Community of Madrid is an autonomous community with its own government and regional public contracting, and the City of Madrid runs its own procurement, both of which publish contract awards that are useful lawful sources.

local_context.title: Financial regulators
local_context.text: Spain's securities regulator, the CNMV, and the Banco de Espana have their head offices in Madrid, and the Madrid stock exchange is the country's main trading venue. Published sanctions, registers of authorised entities and significant shareholding disclosures are important in due diligence on listed companies, banks and investment firms; supervisory files are confidential.

tdsc_approach: For matters touching Madrid, TDSC first establishes the forum and the type of proceeding, whether a commercial court in Madrid, a criminal matter before the national courts, an arbitration administered in the city or enforcement elsewhere against Madrid assets, because that governs which records counsel can obtain and how findings should be documented. Research draws on Mercantile Registry filings and gazette publications, regulator and procurement publications, published judgments and open sources, reviewed under the GDPR and Spanish data protection law. Property information is obtained through counsel or registry procedures. Where interviews or field inquiries in Madrid are required, TDSC coordinates private detectives authorised under Spanish law and works with the client's Spanish counsel. TDSC has no office in Madrid.

faqs.q: Can TDSC support an arbitration administered in Madrid?
faqs.a: Yes, as a consultant to counsel. TDSC can research counterparties, profile witnesses and experts and identify assets relevant to enforcement in arbitrations administered by the Madrid international centre or by domestic institutions in the city. Counsel and the tribunal decide how material is used, and work is documented for possible later court review.

faqs.q: Why do so many Spanish fraud cases appear before courts in Madrid?
faqs.a: The Audiencia Nacional, seated in Madrid, has nationwide jurisdiction over certain serious offences, including large frauds affecting the national economy or several provinces. Major corporate fraud and corruption cases are therefore often handled there. TDSC reviews published decisions and press coverage of such proceedings as part of background research, without access to sealed files.

faqs.q: How does TDSC find out what a party owns in Madrid?
faqs.a: TDSC maps companies and directorships through Mercantile Registry filings and gazette notices and builds a picture of likely holdings from open sources. Formal property information in Spain comes from the Property Registries, which counsel can request in the proper form. Together these support enforcement strategy developed by Spanish lawyers.

faqs.q: Can TDSC screen counterparties for Madrid public contracts?
faqs.a: Yes. TDSC screens bidders, partners and intermediaries for ownership opacity, prior exclusions or sanctions, adverse litigation and links to politically exposed persons, using company filings, published contract awards from national, regional and municipal bodies, court decisions and media. Findings support compliance decisions and are not a substitute for legal advice.

faqs.q: Does TDSC have an office or investigators in Madrid?
faqs.a: No. TDSC has no office, staff or address in Madrid or elsewhere in Spain. Engagements are run from Nashville. Where a matter needs local inquiries, TDSC coordinates independent private detectives holding the required Spanish authorisation and works with the client's Spanish counsel within an agreed written scope.
